papers.title: AI4BayesCode: From Natural Language Descriptions to Validated Modular Stateful Bayesian Samplers
papers.abstract: Coding and computation remain major bottlenecks in Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) workflows, especially as modern sampling algorithms have become increasingly complex and existing probabilistic programming systems remain limited in model support, extensibility, and composability. We introduce AI4BayesCode, an extensible LLM-driven system that translates natural-language Bayesian model descriptions into runnable, validated MCMC samplers. To improve reliability, AI4BayesCode adopts a modular design that decomposes models into modular sampling blocks and maps each block to a built-in sampling component, reducing the need to implement complex sampling algorithms from scratch. Reliability is further improved through pre-generation validation of model specifications and post-generation validation of generated sampler code. AI4BayesCode also introduces a novel recursively stateful coding paradigm for MCMC, allowing modular sampling components, potentially developed by different contributors, to be composed coherently within larger MCMC procedures. We develop a benchmark suite to evaluate AI4BayesCode for sampler-generation. Experiments show that AI4BayesCode can implement a wide range of Bayesian models from natural-language descriptions alone. As an open-ended system, its capability can continue to expand with improvements in the underlying AI agent and the addition of new built-in blocks. The software is available at https://ai4bayescode.com/.

papers.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
papers.abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

papers.title: Compressed Simulation-Based Inference: Neural Posterior Estimation for Massive Data via Low-Dimensional Sketches
papers.abstract: Neural posterior estimation (NPE) is a popular Bayesian simulation-based inference (SBI) approach that uses neural networks trained on simulated data--parameter pairs to approximate the posterior given a user-chosen prior. For high-dimensional observations, NPE methods typically approximate the conditional density of the parameter given a user-chosen or learned summary statistic, rather than the entire dataset, due to the curse of dimensionality. However, both approaches face challenges: hand-crafting good summaries for complex models requires considerable effort from scientists, while learning them from massive datasets can be prohibitively computationally expensive. To address these challenges, we propose approximating the conditional density of a parameter given low-dimensional sketches of the data. We show that, for a model with a $p$-dimensional parameter, only $2p+1$ random sketches are needed for posterior consistency. We compare with state-of-the-art embedding networks for NPE, and we find that our method \emph{matches} the best embedding network's performance while \emph{increasing computational efficiency}.

papers.title: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
papers.abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $\mu(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((\kappa^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

papers.title: Network sampling: a comparative review
papers.abstract: Network sampling is essential for the study of real world systems, since access to the topological structure and dynamical characteristics of a complex system is usually infeasible, and can also prove computationally intractable for large and dense networks. However, the field still lacks systematic methodologies that allow a procedural analysis of sampling plans for connected data. Hence, this study aims to compare network sampling methods through the usage of multivariate statistical analysis and machine learning techniques that are anchored in network metrics' estimation of synthetic and real-world networks. It was demonstrated that no single sampling strategy dominates both cases, although Forest fire and Frontier sampling have presented the most consistent performance across all topologies investigated. The impact of each structural property of these networks for principal component analysis and classification results were also discussed, with consistent pattern groups seen for both data types. Transfer learning aimed at real-world network identification has also demonstrated that realistic structural connections can be correlated to well-known network models through the usage of sampled subgraphs' properties for model training, providing an avenue to real-world network characterization through sampling methodologies.

papers.title: Certified Algorithms for Gaussian Location Mixture NPMLEs via Discretized Gradient Flows
papers.abstract: We study the computation of approximate nonparametric maximum likelihood estimators (NPMLEs) for Gaussian location mixtures in arbitrary dimension $d\ge 1$ via the Fisher-Rao gradient flow. We provide a certified algorithm based on an entropic proximal discretization of the flow which, given a sufficiently small $\varepsilon > 0$, returns an absolutely continuous mixing measure $\tilde\mu$ admitting an exact finite-dimensional representation and satisfying $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\tilde\mu})\le\varepsilon$. For almost every dataset $X_1,\cdots, X_n \in \mathbb{R}^d$ satisfying $n>2(d+1)(m+1)^2$, where $m$ is the number of support points of the NPMLE, the algorithm requires $O(n\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d+2}(1/\varepsilon))$ time. En route, we also establish results on the well-posedness and convergence properties of the continuous-time Fisher--Rao flow. In particular, initializing the flow at the uniform probability measure on a ball containing the convex hull of the observations, we show that $\hat L_n-L_n(f_{\mu_t})=O(\log t/t)$. We also establish that, for almost every dataset satisfying the same condition on $n$ as above, the set of global maxima of the optimal score is the same as the support of the NPMLE, and the Hessian of the optimal score is nondegenerate at these points, extending a result of (Polyanskiy-Sellke, 2025) to higher dimensions.

papers.title: Computing rare events in L\'evy-driven systems via optimal control
papers.abstract: We extend the optimal control formulation of sample path large deviation theory, which has proven effective for numerical computation of instantons and sharp probability estimates in stochastic differential equations with Gaussian noise, to systems with light-tailed L\'evy noise. In the scaling limit of small jumps and high intensity, such systems satisfy a large deviation principle of Freidlin-Wentzell type, with a running cost given by the Legendre transform of the noise cumulant generating function. We propose to numerically minimize this cost over noise realizations subject to the system dynamics, which yields the instanton without having to solve Hamilton's equations, and naturally handles degenerate and multiplicative noise. When the cumulant generating function has a bounded domain, the cost grows only linearly for large noise, and instantons can contain jumps. We analyze when jumps are not only admissible but optimal, depending on the subleading behavior of the cost and on the drift, and show how jumps can be resolved numerically through a time reparameterization that freezes physical time. For continuous instantons, we derive Riccati and Fredholm determinant expressions for the leading-order prefactor, and we discuss the modifications needed when the instanton jumps. We illustrate and validate our methods against Monte Carlo simulations in several examples: a two-dimensional nonlinear model, an active run-and-tumble particle with non-Gaussian tumbling noise, and the Ghil-Sellers energy balance climate model with L\'evy-perturbed solar forcing.

papers.title: Conditional Stochastic User Equilibrium as a Gibbs Distribution: Tractable Flow Laws and Exact Path-Free Sampling
papers.abstract: Treating traffic counts as data calls for the joint distribution of link flows. Stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) gives a single flow vector, and independent route choice at fixed probabilities ignores congestion feedback between travelers. Conditional stochastic user equilibrium (CSUE), in which each traveler of a finite population chooses a route by logit conditional on the routes of all others, contains this feedback but has been hard to compute with at scale. Under separable link costs and a common route-choice precision, the CSUE conditionals are those of a unique Gibbs distribution whose energy is a left-endpoint discrete congestion potential, and for continuous nondecreasing costs the law concentrates on deterministic logit SUE in the large-population limit. When the routes of each origin are the paths of an acyclic bush, retaining origin- or OD-level labels gives an unnormalized layered link-flow law with an explicit product-form multiplicity. On this representation we build a block Metropolis-Hastings sampler whose proposal is an integer version of Dial's loading under frozen costs. It leaves the CSUE law on the bush route sets invariant without enumerating paths or storing individual routes, and at stationarity the mean rejection rate of a block lies between one and two times the total variation distance between its proposal and exact conditional. In experiments, the sampler reproduces reference laws from exact enumeration and traveler-level Gibbs sampling, whereas independent route choice at frozen costs reproduces mean flows but overstates link-flow standard deviations by up to 48% and distorts correlations. On Sioux Falls, the block sampler attains 76.1 times the minimum effective sample size per CPU second of traveler-level Gibbs sampling, and on Chicago Sketch, with over one million travelers, its sampled covariance is used to assess traffic-count locations.

papers.title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
papers.abstract: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

papers.title: Nonlinear Joint State and Noise Estimation under Packet Dropouts and Additive Measurement Corruption
papers.abstract: This paper investigates joint state and noise covariance estimation for nonlinear systems subject to dual reliability impairments: random packet dropouts and additive measurement corruption. This scenario poses challenging nonconjugate inference, as clean and corrupted measurements share an unknown baseline covariance $\boldsymbol{R}_k$ with fixed known corruption covariance $\boldsymbol{E}_k$. Packet reception is observable, whereas the authenticity of received measurements remains latent and must be inferred. To resolve this intractable estimation problem, we cast joint posterior inference as a variational optimization problem and develop a conjugate variational inference adaptive Kalman filter with dual reliability (CVIAKF-DR). The proposed method retains analytical updates for the prediction covariance and two reliability probabilities, while adopting CVI to estimate the state and baseline measurement covariance. The covariance update combines the analytical contribution from clean measurements with Monte Carlo gradient estimates for corrupted measurements. Numerical results on a re-entry tracking benchmark demonstrate the superior accuracy of the proposed method in both state and noise covariance estimation. Remarkably, even built upon the linear Kalman filtering (KF) framework that is originally designed for linear systems, our method achieves more accurate estimation performance than dedicated nonlinear filtering algorithms based on the cubature Kalman filter (CKF).

papers.title: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
papers.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

papers.title: An Analytic Two-Dimensional Benchmark for Integrated Autocorrelation Times in Branching Monte Carlo Part I: Transport Spectra and Branching Theory
papers.abstract: Predicting correlations between source generations can support uncertainty estimation and variance reduction in Monte Carlo transport. We derive a two-dimensional benchmark for planar isotropic exponential flights in a reflecting square. An image construction gives the exact collision and absorption spectra. Critical branching preserves the mean transport operator but changes mode covariances through the offspring second moment. These covariances give tally autocorrelations and integrated autocorrelation times, with a large-population, finite-window approximation for normalized source tallies. Direct Monte Carlo measurements test the predictions for absorption/rebirth and two-offspring fission. The benchmark provides a reference for assessing reduced correlation models, for correcting reported tally uncertainties, and for checking the tallies of a production code for correlation bias.

papers.title: Two-Stage Staffing with Random Arrival Rate: A Simulation Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: In service systems, the arrival rate in the same time period and day of the week exhibits randomness, yet can be more accurately estimated or forecast right before that period, which motivates a two-stage staffing scheme with advance base staffing and pre-shift surge staffing. Existing approaches usually impose strong assumptions on the arrival process and service systems' operational logic and other further approximations (i.e., stylized models) to derive explicit staffing policies. This paper proposes a simulation optimization approach (SOA) for more general arrival processes and service systems by effectively addressing some intertwined challenges. By recasting the original formulation into computationally tractable structures and designing an efficient coordinate-search algorithm, it constructs a two-stage staffing lookup table offline, which allows managers to make real-time surge staffing decisions without any further simulation. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SOA has significantly better staffing performance and substantially broader applicability compared to existing approaches. Even under the stylized models, the cost savings delivered by our SOA compared with existing approaches range from the low tens to several tens of percent, depending on different problem parameters; the advantage further amplifies when the actual problem deviates from the stylized models. In a nurse-staffing case study grounded in real-world data, the proposed SOA delivers approximately 8% to 13% cost savings over a state-of-the-art benchmark.

papers.title: Estimation of Heterogeneous and Functional Cox Model
papers.abstract: Cox or proportional hazards model is the most commonly used regression model for failure time data and has been extended in various ways. In this paper, we consider inference for a heterogeneous and functional Cox model with the focus on estimation of the latent heterogeneous or subgroup structure based on interval-censored failure time data. For the problem, we propose a novel sieve maximum likelihood estimation procedure with the uses of B-splines and Bernstein polynomials. For the implementation of the proposed method, an EM algorithm is developed and the number of subgroups can be determined in a data-driven manner. Also the resulting estimators are shown to be consistent and asymptotically normal, and an extensive simulation study shows that the proposed method works well in practice. Finally, we apply it to an Alzheimer's Disease study that motivated this investigation and provide some new insights about the roles of imaging and clinical factors in the progression of Alzheimer's disease.

papers.title: Count Constraints and Conditional Benchmarks for Roster-Based Network Reconstruction
papers.abstract: When everyone reports contact counts for known groups, roster-based aggregated relational data (ARD) can determine individual links. In our sparse circular design with 40 nodes and eight groups, the complete counts fix 35.6% of realized edges on average. Zero counts alone exclude 91.1% of nonedges on average, and the full set of counts raises that share to 91.7%. We assess ranking on the unresolved pairs by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Uniform weighting of compatible graphs yields higher mean AUC than the direct scores from either a circular latent-position fit or a nuclear-norm fit. In a follow-up analysis, using the same fitted probabilities to weight compatible graphs reverses the comparison for the circular fit. With the generating circular form and interaction strength supplied, its mean AUC exceeds uniform by 0.016-0.019 across three paired density settings. The gain is 0.007 under a stochastic blockmodel, where the circular form is misspecified. Nuclear-norm plug-in scores remain below uniform in mean AUC. For independent Bernoulli edges with fixed probabilities strictly between zero and one, we characterize when an oracle using the true probabilities gives the same edge marginals as uniform weighting for every feasible count array. This occurs exactly when the conditional graph law is uniform on every such array, or equivalently when log odds are additive in node-by-group effects. We recommend reporting fixed edge states, ranking on unresolved pairs, and generating-probability error separately.

papers.title: orderStatMoments: Exact Means, Variances, and Covariances of Order Statistics in R
papers.abstract: Calculating the moments, i.e., means, variances, and covariances, of the order statistics of a sample is critical, as they are foundations for order-statistics-based estimation and inference problems. In the early literature, the exact covariance matrices were tabulated only up to the sample size of 50 under normality. Recent software either provides exact calculation only for the means and variances of single order statistics, or obtains the covariances by approximations. We create the R package orderStatMoments to calculate the exact values of these moments for any ranks and any sample size. It covers thirteen built-in distribution families, specified by name and parameters as in R, and allows for continuous distributions defined by the user under relatively weak conditions. It also calculates the moments of any linear combination of order statistics, including sample quantiles, and Lloyd's best linear unbiased estimators with their variances. The work makes two contributions. First, the package provides the exact covariances between order statistics, which no software we found does. Second, we design methods based on the statistical properties of order statistics critical for ultra accurate computing at large sample sizes and various distributions. The accuracy is verified against closed forms at sample sizes up to $n = 10^6$, against the permutation identities on full matrices, and against 556 cells tabulated in seven publications, where it identified some errors far beyond the stated accuracy. A comparison with five R packages and Python's SciPy shows advantages of this package. Computing is efficient, with a time nearly independent of the sample size.

papers.title: Bayesian variable selection via collapsed importance-weighted variational inference over discrete model spaces
papers.abstract: Bayesian variable selection under spike-and-slab priors provides interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities for individual predictors, but exploring large discrete model spaces using conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be computationally challenging. We develop a collapsed importance-weighted variational framework for Gaussian linear regression. The framework analytically integrates out the remaining model parameters and directly approximates the posterior over binary inclusion indicators using a factorised Bernoulli distribution. To improve posterior inclusion probability estimation while retaining the computational simplicity of the factorised variational family, we replace the conventional evidence lower bound with a tighter variational R\'enyi importance-weighted lower bound. We establish a finite-sample upper bound on posterior inclusion probability approximation errors and show that, under suitable conditions, the optimised variational inclusion probabilities converge to their exact posterior counterparts as the number of importance samples increases and the R\'enyi parameter decreases appropriately. We further establish that analytical marginalisation tightens the variational objective and the corresponding inclusion probability error bound, while reducing importance-weight variance and improving the asymptotic efficiency of importance-sampling post-processing. To address the challenges of estimating gradients with respect to the variational parameters when the inclusion indicators are discrete, we leverage recent advances in variance-reduced score-function estimators, together with an annealing strategy to stabilise optimisation. Simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate improvements in posterior inclusion probability estimation relative to standard variational inference and two existing variational approaches.

papers.title: tsspiral: An R Package to Create Circular Versions of Time Series Plots
papers.abstract: `tsspiral` is an open-source R package that introduces a circular approach to time series visualisation using polar coordinates. We refer to this circular representation of time series data as a spiral. `tsspiral` provides a collection of `ggplot2` geometries for creating a spiral representation of time series data. In our approach, we arrange observations around a circle. Each year is represented by a circle, with the angular position corresponding to the day of the year, and successive years appear as concentric rings. This arrangement facilitates the exploration of periodicity, seasonality, and recurring temporal patterns, particularly in long time series. The package also supports temporal hierarchical visualisations to compare patterns across time scales. By bringing polar-coordinate-based visualisation into routine time series analysis, `tsspiral` offers a practical tool for exploring temporal patterns and communicating complex time-dependent structures. Rather than treating spiral plots as standalone graphics, our approach brings them into the grammar of graphics framework, enabling users to explore temporal patterns through a broader range of visual encodings.

papers.title: Function-on-function nonlinear autoregressive model (F2NARX) for probabilistic surrogate modeling of stochastic dynamical systems
papers.abstract: Constructing accurate and computationally efficient surrogate models for predicting dynamical system responses is critical in many engineering domains, yet remains challenging due to the strongly nonlinear and high-dimensional mapping from external excitations and system parameters to system responses. This work introduces a novel Function-on-Function Nonlinear AutoRegressive model with eXogenous inputs (F2NARX), which reformulates the recently proposed $\mathcal{F}$-NARX method from a function-on-function regression perspective. The proposed framework substantially improves predictive efficiency while maintaining high accuracy. By combining principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression, F2NARX further enables probabilistic predictions of dynamical responses via the unscented transform in an autoregressive manner. The effectiveness of the method is demonstrated through case studies of varying complexity. Results show that F2NARX outperforms state-of-the-art NARX model by orders of magnitude in efficiency while achieving higher accuracy in general. The probabilistic prediction capability of F2NARX is further demonstrated by combining it with active learning for first-passage probability estimation, showing its potential for reliability-oriented applications.

papers.title: A Hybrid NUTS-Gibbs Sampler with State Space Marginalization for Estimation of Dynamic Structural Equation Models with Binomial Outcomes
papers.abstract: Dynamic structural equation models (DSEMs) are widely used for analyzing intensive longitudinal data (ILD). Although many ILD have categorical (Bernoulli or binomially distributed) responses, currently available algorithms for estimating DSEMs are limited to using the probit link and the Bernoulli distribution, i.e., the response can only be success or failure for a single trial and not the number of successes in multiple trials. They also scale poorly with increasing model complexity and sample size. Here, we present a hybrid sampler---alternating between one step of the No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) and one Gibbs step---which solves both of these problems: the Gibbs step naturally handles P\'olya-Gamma distributed latent variables arising from binomially distributed responses with a logit link, and the NUTS step utilizes a Kalman filter to exactly marginalize over latent states, making models with dynamics defined in terms of latent traits more computationally feasible. We demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed sampler in simulation experiments, and also study conditions under which it fails. We finally illustrate its use in an example application of predicting panic attacks.

papers.title: Spectral divide-and-conquer MCMC for long stationary time series
papers.abstract: Bayesian inference via Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods can be prohibitively slow for long time series. Distributed Bayesian inference across multiple cores or machines is non-trivial since simple data splits in time perform badly under temporal dependence. We show that a systematic partitioning of the periodogram observations in the frequency domain gives a fast and accurate posterior approximation for stationary series that can also be used when the computations exceed the memory capacity of a single computational node. Our method uses the asymptotic independence of periodogram observations in the Whittle likelihood to develop a distributed fast Fourier transform combined with embarrassingly parallel Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms in modern cluster-computing frameworks. We establish that the error of the spectral divide-and-conquer MCMC posterior approximation relative to the exact time-domain posterior converges to zero in probability in a shrinking neighbourhood of the full-data Whittle posterior mode. The proposed method is shown to be competitive with the current state-of-the-art distributed MCMC for time series when dependence is weak, and substantially more accurate in a highly persistent setting. The methodology is used to perform a rolling forecast evaluation of one-second market liquidity costs from histories of up to 24 million observations.

papers.title: postshock: An R Package for Donor-Adjusted Forecasting After Structural Shocks
papers.abstract: We present the postshock R package, which implements and extends a donor-based framework for forecasting when a structural shock is known and the target response of interest is not yet observed. The package estimates shock effects from historical donor episodes, balances donors using specified matching features, and transfers the resulting adjustment to a target-series forecast. It provides integrated workflows for conditional mean forecasting through ARIMA and ARIMAX models and conditional variance forecasting through GARCH-X models. Additional functionality includes structured donor pools, control-shock regressors, automated GARCH-X order selection, processed data objects, and reproducible empirical workflows.

papers.title: Local Whittle estimation for distributional time series: A regularization framework in Bayes Hilbert space
papers.abstract: We study local Whittle estimation of long memory in density-valued time series in Bayes Hilbert space. The centered log-ratio (clr) transformation maps densities to a linear Hilbert space, allowing analysis using standard Hilbert space methods. When densities are reconstructed from finite samples, however, small absolute estimation errors can remain large relative to the true density in low-density tails. Taking logarithms can amplify this noise and introduce systematic distortions that affect memory estimation. We develop a framework for regularizing estimated densities before transformation to improve finite-sample performance while preserving the latent memory target. Using the clr representation, we apply local Whittle estimation to principal component scores along an estimated leading direction of the long-run covariance operator. The framework is based on local Whittle admissibility, defined by uniform asymptotic equivalence between the feasible and latent-score criteria. We separate density-estimation error from the population perturbation induced by regularization and give sufficient admissibility conditions based on density-estimation rates and the temporal dependence of the error components. Under suitable regularity assumptions, these conditions yield consistency for the latent memory parameter. We study additional tail smoothing, a vanishing density floor, and their combination. Monte Carlo experiments show that these procedures can reduce finite-sample bias relative to unregularized kernel density reconstruction. An application to daily distributions of intraday EUR/USD exchange rate returns illustrates the methodology.
